What was the BASIC prompt character on the Apple IIe?
Short answer: ] — the closing bracket, used by Applesoft BASIC, which shipped in ROM on the Apple IIe.
What was the BASIC prompt character on the Apple IIe?

The > character was the prompt for Integer BASIC (also called "Integer" or "Apple Integer BASIC"), the original BASIC on the Apple I and Apple II. Integer BASIC was not included in the Apple IIe ROM; it required a Language Card with the Integer ROM.
What was the BASIC prompt character on the Apple IIe?
So both characters appear in Apple II history, but on the IIe the default power-on BASIC prompt was ].

Can I add something to the Apple Wallet for my iPhone from my MacBook if I'm logged in to the same Apple account on both?
Distinguish passes/tickets (boarding passes, event tickets, coupons) from payment cards (debit/credit for Apple Pay); Apple documents them differently.
Can I add something to the Apple Wallet for my iPhone from my MacBook if I'm logged in to the same Apple account on both?
Can I add something to the Apple Wallet for my iPhone from my MacBook if I'm logged in to the same Apple account on both?

It depends what “something” is. Being signed in with the same Apple Account on both devices is necessary for several Wallet-related features, but it does not mean every Wallet item you add on the Mac automatically appears on the iPhone.
Can I add something to the Apple Wallet for my iPhone from my MacBook if I'm logged in to the same Apple account on both?

Passes and tickets (non–payment “Wallet passes”) — Often yes. Apple documents adding passes (for example boarding passes or movie tickets) from Safari on Mac to Wallet on iPhone, iPad, iPod touch, or Mac, and says iCloud must be set up for Safari on the iPhone (iOS 6 or later) or Mac. You open the pass in Safari on the Mac, use Add to Wallet (or Update if the pass changed). Mail on Mac can similarly surface passes you add toward Wallet on iPhone when iCloud is set up on both devices (see Apple’s Mail User Guide for your macOS version).
Can I add something to the Apple Wallet for my iPhone from my MacBook if I'm logged in to the same Apple account on both?

Debit/credit and other Apple Pay payment cards — Not by simple cross-device sync. To use Apple Pay on more than one device, Apple’s Set up Apple Pay guidance is to add the card in Wallet (or Wallet & Apple Pay settings) on each device you want to pay from, then complete any bank or card issuer verification for that device. The same Apple Account helps (and Cards Found For You / similar flows can reuse cards you already added elsewhere so you are not retyping everything), but the card is still enrolled per device for security, not copied automatically as a fully active card everywhere.
Can I add something to the Apple Wallet for my iPhone from my MacBook if I'm logged in to the same Apple account on both?

Practical takeaway — For tickets/passes from the web or email, adding on the Mac in Safari or Mail is a normal path and can land in Wallet on the iPhone when iCloud requirements are met. For paying in stores or with Apple Pay cards, plan to add (or re-verify) the card on the iPhone even if it is already on the Mac.

Software architecture names the major structures of a software system—the parts, their responsibilities, and the rules governing how they relate—so that the system stays understandable, evolvable, and fit for its quality goals (performance, security, operability, cost, etc.).
It is not only diagrams; it is the set of decisions that are costly to reverse plus the shared mental model a team uses when changing the system.
Sits between product intent and implementation detail: narrower than “everything about the system,” broader than a single module or framework choice.
Overlaps with design and engineering leadership; in many organisations, “architecture” highlights cross-cutting or long-lived choices (integration, data ownership, deployment shape, failure modes).
Common views and notations include the C4 model, ADRs (Architecture/Decision/Record), and architecture-as-code tools such as Structurizr—each answers different audiences and lifecycles.
Stakeholder fit — Architecture is good only relative to stated drivers (latency, compliance, team topology, time-to-market); there is no universal “best” shape.
Constraints and trade-offs — Prefer explicit trade-off language over buzzwords; every important gain usually costs something elsewhere.
Integrity over time — Guard boundaries, interfaces, and invariants so incremental work does not silently erode the model.
Practitioners capture architecture through models (structural, deployment, runtime), records (ADRs, RFCs), reviews, and linting or validation in code when possible.
Refactoring and strangling legacy areas are architecture work as much as greenfield diagrams.
Choosing sync vs async integration between bounded areas; defining service or module boundaries aligned with team ownership.
Publishing a container-level diagram for onboarding and incident response; using C4 context + container views as the default communication set.
“Architecture = ivory tower before coding” — Often false; healthy architecture is continuously refined as the system and risks become visible.
“One UML diagram is enough” — Usually insufficient; different stakeholders need different abstractions (see C4/Diagram for a structured split).
“Microservices = good architecture” — Oversimplified; distribution is a cost you pay for specific scaling or organisational goals, not a quality in itself.
A tell (from Arabic tall, “mound, small hill”) is an artificial mound: stratified debris from many successive settlements built on the same footprint, plus natural sediment—not a natural hill.

Tells are the signature landform of multi-period occupation in archaeology: each layer encodes a phase of building, abandonment, and rebuilding, so the mound is both a landscape feature and a vertical archive of human use.
Tells are most strongly associated with the ancient Near East (Upper Mesopotamia, Southern Levant, Anatolia, Iran) where continuous settlement in less arid zones allowed debris to outpace erosion.
The pattern also appears in Southern and Central Europe (e.g. Greece, Bulgaria, Hungary, Spain), North Africa, and West Africa—anywhere accumulation can win over truncation.
In the Southern Levant, the tell-dominated settlement pattern largely ends with the Hellenistic shift after Alexander the Great; elsewhere many tells remain occupied today.
English tell entered archaeological usage in the 1840s; field spellings include tel, tall, til, and tal depending on source language and transliteration convention.
Stratified time depth — Superimposed cultural layers (often labeled by period or phase) make tells prime targets for stratigraphic excavation.
Net accumulation — A tell forms only when deposition exceeds removal (erosion, deliberate leveling, modern earthmoving); that constraint explains the tell’s geographic clustering.

Terminology is regional — Equivalent mound words include tepe / tappeh (Turkish/Persian), hüyük / höyük (Turkish), kom (Egyptian Arabic), and chogha (Persian); khirbet (“ruin”) often labels ruined tells in toponyms but is not synonymous with tell.
Toponymy — Tell is among the most common prefixes in Palestinian place names; the same root appears in biblical Hebrew tel and in Akkadian/Sumerian cognates debated by philologists.
Mound material mixes organic and cultural refuse, collapsed mudbrick and other building rubble, water-laid and aeolian sediments, and residues of biogenic and geochemical processes on site.
The classic profile is a low truncated cone with sloping sides and a flat, mesa-like summit; large examples exceed 40 m in height and can cover tens of hectares at the base.

A tell is not born as a mound: the earliest occupation is a flat surface; nucleation of households and repeated rebuilding of daub structures over generations raises the horizon—often over centuries before the form reads clearly as a tell.

Near East — Tell es-Sultan (Jericho) among the earliest known examples; Tell Barri in Syria; the Citadel of Aleppo atop a tell occupied since the third millennium BCE; Tel Megiddo in Israel. Surveys have cataloged thousands of tells in the Southern Levant alone.

Europe — Neolithic and Chalcolithic tells in northeastern Bulgaria; Greek toumbas (Macedonia) and magoulas (Thessaly), with debate over communal nucleation (Chapman) versus household-scale accumulation (Halstead).
Scale — Tell Barri reaches on the order of 30+ m height with a large basal footprint, illustrating how long occupation can dominate local topography.
“Every prominent hill in the Levant is a tell” — False; relief must be explained by anthropogenic buildup and stratified settlement, not geology alone.
“Tell and tel are interchangeable spellings for one language” — Oversimplified; tel often marks Hebrew toponym transliteration, tell Arabic—same concept, different conventions.
“A tell is always abandoned” — False; many tells are still lived on; khirbet (“ruin”) in a name signals destruction, not the tell concept itself.
“You can date a tell from its exterior shape alone” — False; chronology comes from excavation, survey, and material culture in strata, not from silhouette.

Markdown Architectural Decision Records (MADR, pronounced like English “matter” ) are a lean Markdown template for capturing architecturally significant decisions—each record documents one architectural decision (AD) and its rationale. The project positions “architecture” broadly: technology choices, tooling, libraries, or product behavior can qualify if they affect the system enough to warrant a structured record.
Repository: github.com/adr/madr — template files, releases, changelog, rendered decision examples (source)
Development template (moving target): adr-template.md on develop
Peer-reviewed write-up: Markdown Architectural Decision Records: Format and Tool Support (ZEUS 2018)
License: dual MIT or CC0 1.0; SPDX: MIT OR CC0-1.0

General ADR practice is wider than one file format; this page anchors the MADR-specific file shape, filenames, and optional YAML metadata used in the official template. For motivation and team pitfalls around ADRs, start from Architecture/Decision/Record.
Top matter (optional): YAML for site generators—e.g. title, status, date, decision-makers, consulted, informed (see live template).
Title (#): short title of the solved problem and chosen solution.
Context and Problem Statement — situation and the question to settle (links to issues/boards welcome).
Considered Options — bullet list of alternatives.
Confirmation (optional) — how you verify the decision (reviews, tests, ArchUnit-style checks, etc.).
Pros and Cons of the Options — per-option Good / Neutral / Bad bullets.
More Information (optional) — evidence, links to superseding ADRs, revisit triggers.

Layout: create docs/decisions (or another root; MADR does not mandate repo layout). Copy contents of the template/ folder into that directory—includes adr-template.md, lint config, and ancillary files.
npm: install published package and copy template:

New decision file: copy adr-template.md to NNNN-title-with-dashes.md (consecutive NNNN, lowercase dashed title, .md suffix); convention is documented as ADR-0005. Other filename schemes exist in the wider ADR community but may break tooling.
Linting: Markdown style can drift; the repo ships .markdownlint config and an example GitHub Actions workflow using markdownlint.
Optional subdirectory per category (e.g. decisions/backend/, decisions/ui/); numbering is then per category, not globally unique—see ADR-0010 and the categories discussion.
